newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Investors seen awaiting stability in new Congo.
newsitem.headline: Investors seen awaiting stability in new Congo.

text.p: Foreign investors, fearful over alleged refugee massacres by Laurent Kabila's forces, are likely to wait for the new government to prove it can maintain political stability before sinking money into the country, analysts and investors told Reuters on Friday.
"People look for reasons not to invest before they look for reasons to invest," said Bill Coogan, managing director of Rothschild Inc and part of a visiting investment delegation.
"News reports about mass graves and refugee massacres are impacting on the American public. It's hard to put those pictures out of your mind," he added.

But delegation members added that investors were hungrily eyeing the mineral-rich country and that political risk was perceived to have lessened since Kabila overthrew the regime of Mobutu Sese Seko last month.
"What you're seeing in (Zaire) is astonishing potential but unquantifiable risk. Making commitments of large amounts of capital is fairly daunting.
"Nevertheless, the political risk has fallen since the demise of Mobutu," said John Clemmow, investment banker at South Africa's Investec Bank.
The new Congo has vast copper, cobalt and zinc resources, as well as gold, diamonds and tin.

In the mid-1980s the country produced some 500,000 tonnes of copper a year, but last year output was only 40,000 tonnes. Cobalt output has dropped from 15,000 tonnes a year to around 4,000 tonnes, but this still represents a fifth of world production.

When Kabila's rebel alliance seized control of the southern Katanga Province, centred 0n Lubumbashi, in April international companies scrambled over each other to snatch mining projects and exploration permits.
The Governor of Katanga Province, Gaetan Kakudji, hosted a reception earlier this week for the delegation.
Potential foreign investors mingled with local bankers and entrepreneurs who urged them to invest and promised every assistance possible.
"We must tell you that our small companies are very ready to receive you as investors," said one Lubumbashi businessman.
One international company has already made a commitment -- American Mineral Fields Inc, the first company to be awarded a mining project by Kabila's government.

Under a joint venture agreement with the state mining company Gecamines, AMF has the rights to develop the Kipushi zinc and build a 200,000 tonnes a year zinc smelter, as well as process the vast Kolwezi copper/cobalt tailings.
Analysts and investors said it was easier to consider ploughing money into the new Congo now that Mobutu had gone.

"Political risk is still huge but sharply better. Before, any deal in (Zaire) used to be seen as a deal with Mobutu and people wondered what would happen to their money when he was gone. They knew he would go soon," Clemmow said.
Mobutu ruled the country for 32 years, reducing its economy to tatters. Roads in and around Lubumbashi are shot through with potholes, and working telephone land lines are virtually non-existent.
The new Congo has ample, cheap electricity to power any mining projects, but some power cables running from Lubumbashi to the Kipushi mine were stolen by unpaid soldiers, AMF said.
